youtube_title: If a Monkey Takes the Photo, Who Owns the Copyright? 🦝⚖️
caption: The U.S. Copyright Office won't register works produced by animals — and its own rulebook lists 'a photo taken by a monkey' as an example. Owning the camera isn't the same as being the author.
script: A monkey took a selfie, and the U.S. Copyright Office says it won't register that photo for anyone. [disclaimer] In America, the answer is weird! The U.S. Copyright Office has a rulebook for what it will register. And it says it plainly. The Office will not register stuff made by nature, animals, or plants. Then it gives examples. And they're amazing! A photo taken by a monkey. A painting made by an elephant. Driftwood shaped by the ocean. Even a song that lists the Holy Spirit as the author! The rule is simple. Copyright protects creative work made by humans. Only humans! So imagine you set up a camera, and a monkey grabs it and snaps a picture. You might own the camera. You might own the memory card. But owning the camera doesn't make you the author of a photo the monkey took! The monkey took it. And the monkey can't own it either. Here's the limit. This doesn't mean every photo with an animal in it is free. If a photographer chooses the shot, the angle, and the moment, that's a human author. When a person and an animal both help, the human part gets looked at on its own. And this is just American copyright. Other countries can see it differently. And contracts can still matter. [loop] So the next time a monkey borrows your camera, remember
